title: Montreal mayor walks back 'clumsy' Kraft Dinner comment after major tax hike
summary: A day after the City of Montreal unveiled a budget that featured a property tax average increase of 9.8 per cent — about three times the inflation rate — the mayor is once again on the defensive.

image.caption: Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada, seen here in a photo from Nov. 21, 2025, says her comments were meant to illustrate that the city had to make some tough choices. (Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: A day after the City of Montreal unveiled a budget that featured a property tax average increase of 9.8 per cent — about three times the inflation rate — the mayor is once again on the defensive.
Day after unveiling budget with huge tax increase, mayor once again on the defensive
This time, it's over comments she made about Kraft Dinner.
The property tax increase unveiled on Tuesday was the talk of city hall, as it meant that Montreal homeowners will need to spend an average of $515 more on taxes.
Soraya Martinez Ferrada has insisted the tax increase is necessary to get the city's finances in order and to catch up on much-needed infrastructure work.
During an interview with local media outlet Urbania, the mayor talked about the city's financial struggles and made a comment that has sparked lots of social media backlash.
"We're going through every service to see what we can save. It's like when you make your personal budget: if you know you'll have less money one year, then, you have to make choices," she said.
"Sometimes, you'll have to eat a little more Kraft Dinner because we can't afford filet mignon."

items: Montreal's 'unprecedented' tax hike key to tackling 'infrastructure crisis,' mayor says
Montreal's tax hike is making headlines, but here are other takeaways from the budget

blocks.text: Many comments online suggested the mayor and the city should've found alternative solutions to the city's financial problems instead of imposing such a hefty tax on residents.
In an Instagram story posted on Wednesday, the mayor acknowledged her comments were "clumsy."
"What I wanted to say is the city will have to make choices: Build new parks or fill potholes. I'm going to focus on filling potholes."

A large chunk of the 9.8 per cent average property tax increase will generate money for a new infrastructure fund that will help the city make more cash payments for maintenance and repair work, rather than relying on credit.
This increase means Martinez Ferrada has broken her campaign promise about limiting tax increases to the rate of inflation.
She was sworn in as mayor in November 2025 and this is her administration's second budget.

Antoni Nerestant has been with CBC Montreal since 2015. He's worked as a video journalist, a sports reporter and a web writer, covering everything from Quebec provincial politics to the 2022 Beijing Olympics.
